The Independent National Electoral Commission has reiterated its commitment to ensuring that persons with disabilities are not excluded from participating in the 2027 general elections. The commission said it was strengthening measures to address physical, communication and procedural barriers that prevent persons with disabilities from exercising their electoral rights. The Resident Electoral Commissioner in Gombe State, Umar Gajiram, stated this on Monday through the Administrative Secretary, Fadimatu Bakari, at a sensitisation workshop on disability inclusion, accessibility and electoral interventions held at Hajiya Amina Inuwa Gombe Hall. Gajiram said every Nigerian had the right to participate in elections, irrespective of physical, visual, hearing or other forms of disability. He said, “As an electoral body, INEC recognises that PWDs have the same rights as every other citizen. Their votes matter, their voices matter, and their participation is important to the growth of our democracy.” He explained that the commission had introduced measures, including assistive materials, improved polling unit accessibility, training of electoral officials and collaboration with disability organisations, to promote inclusive elections. However, he cautioned that providing such interventions was not enough without ensuring their effective implementation. “Having these measures in place is not enough. We must ensure that they are properly understood and put into practice. This is why today’s programme brings together PWDs, Electoral Officers and Disability Desk Officers. We want to share information, listen to your experiences, understand the challenges you face and find practical ways of addressing them before the 2027 General Election,” he said. He also charged the Disability Desk Officer to remain accessible to disability groups and ensure that their concerns were communicated to the commission for appropriate action. Gajiram encouraged representatives of persons with disabilities to share their experiences openly and identify areas requiring improvement in the electoral process. “As we look forward to 2027, our goal is simple: to ensure that no eligible Nigerian is left out of the electoral process because of disability. “We want a situation where persons using wheelchairs can easily access polling units, persons with visual impairment can vote with appropriate assistance, persons with hearing impairment can receive election information, and every eligible voter with a disability can vote with dignity and confidence,” he added. He stressed that facilitating the participation of persons with disabilities was not an act of favour but a fundamental right of Nigerian citizens. Also speaking, the Assistant Director, Youth, at INEC headquarters, Bukar Maikwada, said the workshop was organised to strengthen stakeholders’ understanding of disability inclusion and ensure the effective deployment of the commission’s interventions ahead of the 2027 general elections. Maikwada said the participation of persons with disabilities as voters, candidates and election personnel was central to building an inclusive, accessible and credible democracy. He said the commission’s commitment to addressing barriers throughout the electoral cycle was anchored on Section 54 of the Electoral Act, 2026, the Discrimination Against Persons with Disabilities (Prohibition) Act, 2018, and INEC’s Framework on Access and Participation of Persons with Disabilities in the Electoral Process. According to him, the workshop would create awareness about the barriers faced by persons with disabilities and strengthen participants’ understanding of physical, information, communication and procedural accessibility. He listed some of the commission’s interventions to include Braille Ballot Guides for visually impaired voters, EC30 PWD Written Instruction Posters for deaf voters, magnifying glasses for persons with visual impairment and albinism, as well as voter education materials in Braille, jingles, flyers and posters. Maikwada said the training would also equip electoral officers with the knowledge required to determine where, when and how the assistive materials should be deployed. He emphasised the need for effective coordination among INEC officials, the Joint National Association of Persons with Disabilities, Organisations of Persons with Disabilities and cluster heads to ensure that the interventions reached their intended beneficiaries. He further called for inclusive voter education and mobilisation through disability clusters, special schools, camps and settlements, urging JONAPWD to take ownership of sensitisation activities within their respective clusters. “The participation of PWDs as voters, candidates and election personnel is central to an inclusive, accessible, credible and participatory democracy. The Commission therefore remains committed to identifying and addressing barriers across the entire electoral cycle,” he said. On the expected outcome of the workshop, Maikwada said it would provide an opportunity for stakeholders to assess previous elections, identify gaps and develop practical recommendations for implementation at national, state, local government and grassroots levels. He said, “This workshop is about moving from awareness to practical action. The availability of inclusive interventions is only one part; effective deployment, communication, utilisation and monitoring are equally critical areas that should not be taken for granted.” He urged stakeholders to strengthen collaboration and ensure that disability inclusion was treated as a collective responsibility rather than the sole responsibility of INEC. Maikwada expressed confidence that sustained sensitisation, targeted mobilisation, accessibility measures and proper deployment of assistive materials would help deliver a more inclusive and participatory electoral process in 2027. Chima Azubuike
